brief.topic: Why Adding Digits Can Catch a Wrong Answer

s01: Can the digits of a number help check a multiplication, without repeating the whole calculation?
Take two hundred forty seven.
It is two hundreds, four tens, and seven ones.
A hundred leaves remainder one when divided by nine.
So does ten.
Replace each hundred and each ten by one.
The remainder is unchanged.
Our digit sum is thirteen, which leaves remainder four.
The original number also leaves four.
Now check two hundred forty seven times three.
Four times three leaves remainder three.
The proposed answer, seven hundred forty one, has digit sum twelve.
That also leaves three, so it passes this check.
Change the answer to seven hundred forty two.
Its digit sum is thirteen.
The remainders disagree, so this answer must be wrong.
But passing is not proof.
Swap the last two digits of the correct answer.
Seven hundred fourteen has the same digit sum, and passes, even though it is wrong.
The reason is place value.
Every power of ten is one more than a multiple of nine.
Digit sums preserve the remainder, and any error that changes the answer by a multiple of nine can slip through.
A small check catches some mistakes, not all of them.

scenes.narration:
Can the digits of a number help check a multiplication, without repeating the whole calculation?

Take two hundred forty seven. It is two hundreds, four tens, and seven ones. A hundred leaves remainder one when divided by nine. So does ten.

Replace each hundred and each ten by one. The remainder is unchanged. Our digit sum is thirteen, which leaves remainder four. The original number also leaves four.

Now check two hundred forty seven times three. Four times three leaves remainder three. The proposed answer, seven hundred forty one, has digit sum twelve. That also leaves three, so it passes this check.

Change the answer to seven hundred forty two. Its digit sum is thirteen. The remainders disagree, so this answer must be wrong.

But passing is not proof. Swap the last two digits of the correct answer. Seven hundred fourteen has the same digit sum, and passes, even though it is wrong.

The reason is place value. Every power of ten is one more than a multiple of nine. Digit sums preserve the remainder, and any error that changes the answer by a multiple of nine can slip through. A small check catches some mistakes, not all of them.
